chief_complaint: persistent headache, brain fog, and screen sensitivity
hpi_details: A 68-year-old female presents with persistent headache, cognitive fog, and screen sensitivity for several weeks after a concussion.
ideas: She thinks she might have a slow bleed or permanent brain damage from the fall since her thinking hasn't cleared up after several weeks.
concerns: She is worried that her memory issues mean she is slipping into dementia and will no longer be able to care for her grandchildren safely.
expectations: She hopes to get a brain MRI scan to rule out bleeding and a medication to clear the persistent mental cloudiness.

core_concepts: Prompt recognition and structured assessment of Post-Concussion Syndrome is essential for guiding targeted diagnostic workup and clinical decision-making.
A thorough clinical history, baseline risk assessment, and targeted objective testing must be synthesized rather than relying on any single symptom in isolation.
Standard management emphasizes Plan for Concussion Follow-up: Return-to-activity/work accommodations, vestibular physical therapy, adapted to individual patient risk factors and clinical severity.
Diagnostic workup and therapeutic decisions should adhere to established clinical guidelines while accounting for patient-specific comorbidities.

common_misconceptions: Assuming that an atypical or mild presentation rules out Post-Concussion Syndrome.
Relying solely on a single normal laboratory value or imaging result to prematurely exclude pathology.
Equating temporary symptomatic relief with full resolution of the underlying condition without completing standard evaluation.
Misattributing symptoms exclusively to Migraine without completing a comprehensive diagnostic workup.
dangerous_errors: Failing to recognize red-flag features and delaying urgent escalation or emergency intervention.
Prematurely discharging or reassuring the patient before completing appropriate diagnostic assessment.
Initiating empirical treatment without considering major patient contraindications or drug interactions.
Ignoring critical warning signs such as: Worsening symptoms — would suggest a need for re-imaging.

boundaries_and_exceptions: Specific drug dosages, monitoring protocols, and referral criteria must be tailored to organ function, comorbidities, and local hospital pathways.
Atypical presentations in elderly, pediatric, or immunocompromised patients may require lower thresholds for inpatient monitoring and specialist consultation.

must_ask.say: Can you tell me about the head injury that started this?
How is your headache and concentration now?
Does screen time make your symptoms worse?
Do you take any blood thinners or aspirin?
How many weeks or months has this lasted?
How is this affecting school or work?

history.answer: I've had this constant dull headache and trouble thinking clearly for several weeks, especially when looking at screens.
About four weeks ago, I tripped over a rug at home and hit the back of my head on the floor. I felt dazed and saw stars for a minute, but I didn't lose consciousness.
It didn't hit me instantly like a lightning bolt, but rather started as a persistent dull ache a couple of hours after the fall and hasn't gone away.
The headache has been present nearly every day for the past four weeks. I rarely had any headaches before this accident.
It feels like a tight, heavy band stretching across my forehead and both of my temples.
It is a steady, dull pressure rather than a throbbing or sharp stabbing pain. On a scale of one to ten, it usually stays around a four or five.
I wake up with a mild pressure, and it steadily builds up as the day goes on, especially in the afternoon.
Looking at my smartphone, watching television, and bright supermarket lights make it worse. Resting quietly in a dark room with my eyes closed brings some relief.
Yes, staring at a computer screen or phone makes my head throb within minutes, and bright daylight really bothers my eyes.
I feel like I'm moving through a heavy fog, and I can't concentrate on reading or balancing my checkbook like I used to.
I get slightly queasy when the headache flares up, but I haven't thrown up at all.
No, I haven't seen any flashing lights, zigzag lines, or blind spots before the headache.
No, my eyes don't get bloodshot or watery, and my nose doesn't run or get stuffy.
My vision isn't blurry or doubled, and my eyes don't hurt deep inside the sockets.
No, I don't have any weakness in my arms or legs, numbness, tingling, or difficulty speaking.
I feel a bit off-balance when I turn my head quickly, but the room isn't spinning violently.
I've been waking up multiple times during the night, and I feel much more irritable and fatigued than usual.
No, I haven't had any fever, chills, severe neck stiffness, or unexplained skin rashes.
No, my temples aren't tender to touch, my scalp doesn't hurt when I comb my hair, and my jaw doesn't ache when I chew.
No, I don't take aspirin, warfarin, or any other blood-thinning medications.
I tried taking over-the-counter acetaminophen a few times during the first week, but it barely helped, so I stopped taking it.
Mental exertion, loud environments, and lack of sleep trigger the pain, but no specific foods or drinks seem to cause it.
No, nobody else in my house has headaches, and our electric heat and carbon monoxide detector are working fine.
No, I have never had cancer or any problems with my immune system.
It has slowed me down considerably. I can't read for more than fifteen minutes or do my volunteer computer work without feeling exhausted and headachy.

I was wondering if I might have a slow bleed in my head from the bump, because this foggy feeling just isn't going away. I'm terrified that this lingering brain fog is actually early dementia and that I won't be able to watch my grandkids anymore.
I really hope you can order a brain scan to make sure there's no bleeding inside, and give me something to clear my head.
I don't have high blood pressure, diabetes, or any other chronic medical conditions.
I've never had any major surgeries and have never been hospitalized.
I am not taking any prescription drugs, over-the-counter medications, or herbal supplements right now.
No, I have no known allergies to any medications or foods.
I have never smoked cigarettes in my life.
I only have an occasional glass of wine at family dinners, maybe once or twice a month.
I am a retired accountant, and I live with my husband in a quiet single-story house.
There is no family history of migraines, brain tumors, or strokes.

exam.finding: Blood pressure is 124/78 mmHg, pulse 72 beats per minute, respiratory rate 14 breaths per minute, temperature 36.6°C, and oxygen saturation 99% on room air.
Alert and well-groomed elderly female wearing tinted lenses, appears slightly fatigued but in no acute distress.
Pupils are equal, round, and reactive to light; extraocular movements intact without nystagmus; fundoscopy reveals distinct optic disc margins without papilledema.
No tenderness to palpation or percussion over the frontal or maxillary sinuses bilaterally.
Mild tenderness on palpation of the suboccipital and upper cervical paraspinal musculature, with full range of motion and no midline bony tenderness.
Neck is supple without resistance to passive flexion; Kernig and Brudzinski signs are negative.
Alert and fully oriented; mild difficulty with serial sevens and backward digit span, but language, memory registration, and recall are intact.
Cranial nerves II through XII are grossly intact with symmetric facial movement and normal hearing.
Normal muscle bulk and tone, with 5/5 motor strength symmetrically throughout the upper and lower extremities.
Intact and symmetric sensation to light touch and pinprick across all dermatomes and the face.
Biceps, triceps, patellar, and Achilles deep tendon reflexes are 2+ bilaterally, and plantar responses are flexor.
Finger-to-nose and heel-to-shin testing are normal; steady casual gait and negative Romberg test, with slight hesitation during tandem walking.
